title: Gas separation with binary-cooperative heterogeneous membranes

paper_content.abstract: Advanced polymer membranes exhibit competitive performance in gas separation. However, rationally designing a polymer membrane with high gas separation performance and structural robustness simultaneously remains challenging. Herein, we present a microzone interfacial polymerization approach to reconstruct the polymer network through the rearrangement of attached functional groups, forming a heterogeneous structure with a crumpled morphology. Unlike common crumpled membranes with homogeneous structures, the heterogeneous structure with a discovered microphase separation endows the membrane with independent and cooperative dual-function regions. The peaks, with more amides as CO2-philic sites, are functionalized as fast CO2 transport channels, whereas the stress release effect via the deformation process maintains a high free volume. Valleys, with more rigid phenyls, demonstrate both enhanced CO2 diffusion and compaction resistance. The cooperative effects of dual-function regions significantly improve the structural robustness, and the optimized membrane exhibits an approximately 300% increase in CO2 permeance and CO2/N2 selectivity compared with its homogeneous counterparts under 1.0 MPa, which is also one order of magnitude greater than that of state-of-the-art membranes. This approach offers a potential pathway for developing more durable polymer membranes suited for harsh environments, which could expand the range of gas separations feasible with membrane technology.
paper_content.introduction:
Separation processes, such as evaporation and distillation, which are widely used in gas and liquid separations, are energy intensive1. Membrane separation technology, as an alternative, typically consumes an order of magnitude less energy and has attracted extensive interest2-7. Currently, polymer membranes still dominate industrial membranes8-10. Various advanced strategies, focused on designing the membrane structure at the molecular level aimed at increasing the gas diffusion or solubility ability or constructing sub-nanometer channels, are conducted to remarkably improve gas permselectivity11-13. However, gas separation membranes are mostly applied under operating pressure, and the polymer structure is easily destroyed owing to compaction or plasticization effects, which reduces the separation performance despite the high low-pressure performance.

Strengthening the interchain interactions in the polymer network is a common strategy to suppress the movement of polymer segments14, 15. Examples of hydrogen bonds16, metal‒ligand bonds17, and ionic or Coulombic interactions18 are implemented to effectively dissipate energy and protect the original network stability under external stresses. Other strategies, such as interpenetrating multiple networks, including those with prior mechanical rupture, demonstrate similar effects19. However, the introduction of the above interactions inevitably sacrifices the free volume and inhibits the transfer of gas molecules, and is capable of forming crystallization areas as stress concentration sites, which tend to form nonselective defects. Bones or teeth in organisms, with alternating arrangements of inorganic phases (hydroxyapatite) and organic phases (collagen), consistently exhibit mechanical robustness. The cooperative effects of the two phases explain the structural stability, which can effectively release external stresses20-24. Inspired by this, accurately constructing independent and cooperative functions within polymer networks is an effective approach to improve gas separation performance while maintaining structural stability, especially under operation pressure.

Herein, we designed a heterogeneous polymer membrane through reconstruction of the polymer network, which was achieved using a microzone interfacial polymerization (IP) technique. A microphase separation phenomenon was discovered by detecting the distribution of functional groups, whereas the peaks were composed of more amide groups and the valleys had more phenyl groups. The resulting cooperative effect endows the membrane with stress release and compaction resistance abilities and enhances CO2 transport and diffusion abilities. This results in gas separation performance compared with that of state-of-the-art membranes.
paper_content.results:
Construction and characterization of heterogeneous structures

A heterogeneous structure was constructed through a microzone ISP strategy (Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2). In this work, we conducted IP reactions in microzones, i.e., micropores, distributed in a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) layer after immersion in an organic phase solution. The swollen micropores (Supplementary Figs. 3c, 4, 5), formed through solvent-induced swelling mechanism (see Supplementary Fig.4 for details), are conducive to anchoring organic phase monomers (trimesoyl chloride (TMC)) because of the capillary effect instead of remaining on the surface of the PDMS layer (Supplementary Fig. 15). In Supplementary Fig. 6, the non-uniform concentration gradient of TMC monomers in the swelling PDMS was qualitatively analyzed by Raman depth imaging, where the red areas indicate the regions with a relatively high concentration of TMC monomers. The advantages and purpose of microzone IP reactions are threefold. First, compared with the common liquid‒liquid IP process, the construction of microreaction zones is conducive to the uniform distribution of TMC monomers, avoiding the disordered arrangement resulting from interfacial disturbances caused by exothermic reactions. Second, refining the macroscopic liquid‒liquid reactions into numerous microreaction units effectively inhibits the reaction rate, making the IP reactions controllable. Third, the IP reactions, which occur at the microporosity, provide more binding sites to enhance the interaction between the selective polymer layer and the PDMS layer. This simple strategy is able to fabricate large-area heterogeneous membranes with a membrane area of 350 cm2 (Supplementary Fig. 7).

The microphase separation phenomenon in the heterogeneous structure was confirmed by atomic force microscopy-infrared spectroscopy (AFM-IR) (Supplementary Figs. 8, 9). The heterogeneous structures (Fig. 1a) are observed on the basis of the detection groups of amide groups (C=O, C–N) from Fig. 1d2 to Fig. 1f2 and the phenyl groups (C=C, C–H) from Fig. 1d3 to Fig. 1f3. The PT-4 and PT-5 membranes have homogeneous structures (Figs. 1b, 1g2-1h2, and 1g3-1h3). The above results demonstrated that the amide groups mostly accumulated at the peaks rather than at the valleys, whereas the phenyl groups showed the opposite trend. However, this phenomenon cannot be observed using Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 10c. The heterogeneous structure caused by the liquid‒liquid (L‒L) microzone IP reactions (Fig. 1c, Zone-1) can be obtained within a residence time of 160 s, which was deemed the waiting time after pouring out the TMC solution. In this process, the n-hexane in the micropores carries the TMC monomers to the L-L interfaces (Supplementary Fig. 11, Zone-1), which subsequently promotes the IP reactions, forming a convex structure. The heterogeneous structure, reflected as a crumpled morphology, was characterized by AFM (Fig. 1d1-f1, Supplementary Fig. 12a1-c3) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, Supplementary Figs. 13a-c, 14a-c). Beyond 160 s (Fig. 1c, Zone-2), a homogeneous structure with a smooth morphology (Figs. 1g1 and Fig.1h1; Supplementary Figs. 12d1-e3, 13d-e, and 14d-e), shown as PT-4 and PT-5 membranes, was achieved from the liquid‒solid (L‒S) microzone IP reactions (Supplementary Fig. 11, Zone-2), caused by the confined movement of TMC monomers to contact piperazine (PIP) monomers. The membranes fabricated with PIP concentrations of 0.2 and 0.3 wt% are shown in Supplementary Fig. 19 and exhibit the same variation tendency as membranes fabricated with a PIP concentration of 0.1 wt%.

The microphase separation phenomenon is attributed to the change in crosslinking density from the PT-1 to the PT-5 membranes, which was analysed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). As shown in Supplementary Table 1, the degree of crosslinking of heterogeneous membranes (PT-1 to PT-3) is significantly greater than that of homogeneous membranes (PT-4 and PT-5), indicating the formation of dense structures. Moreover, the increase in the O/N ratio from the PT-1 to PT-3 membranes indicates an increase in linear crosslinking structures in the resultant PA membranes. This suggests that the acyl chloride groups on the PDMS surface were partially hydrolysed to form carboxyl groups when in contact with the PIP solution, reducing the crosslinking density. Hence, the composition differences at the peaks and valleys stem from the variations initiated at the micropores and surface on the PDMS layer in the IP processes, which subsequently changed the crosslinking density.

Formation mechanism of heterogeneous structure

The formation mechanism of the heterogeneous structure, explained as the L‒L microzone IP reaction, was illustrated by Raman scanning spectroscopy. We detected different functional groups by adjusting the Raman focusing mode to observe the microphase separation phenomenon. In the autofocus mode, the Raman laser focuses on the highest location of the membrane surface, which is the peak in the crumpled morphology. Discrete red points, representing C=O or C-N groups in the nascent polyamide films (Fig. 2a1), appear at the initial contact of PIP and TMC monomers (Fig. 2a1-1). This produces large polyamide films through continuous IP reactions (Fig. 2a2), as reflected by the dense red points in Fig. 2a2-1. In Fig. 2a3-1, adjacent large polyamide films are capable of decreasing the surface energy, followed by incorporation with other adjacent polyamide films to obtain the final crumpled morphology (Fig. 2a3). In fixed focus mode, the Raman laser is limited to the mPSf surface, which is regarded as the valley in the crumpled morphology. Unlike the results in Fig. 2a1-1 to 2a3-1, dense red points, representing the C=C or C-H groups in Fig. 2a4-1, appear immediately on the mPSf surface, followed by a decrease in density with continuous reaction in Fig. 2a5-1, which indicates the growth of nascent polyamide films (Fig. 2a5). The disappearance of the red points indicates the cavity structure of growing polyamide films. The significant decrease in the red point density in Fig. 2a6-1 reflects the incorporation of polyamide films, which results in peaks with a crumpled morphology corresponding with the results in Fig. 2a3-1. The formation mechanism of the homogeneous structure, as reflected by the smooth morphology, is explained by the L-S IP reaction shown in Fig. 2b. As shown in Fig. 2b1 to Fig. 2b3, the absence of solvents in the micropores makes it difficult to induce TMC to contact PIP consecutively to participate in the IP reaction; therefore, the formed polyamide films are difficult to grow or incorporate further. The final smooth morphology is obtained through the compact packing of polyamide films, which shows the gradual densification of red points in the Raman signals from Fig. 2(b1-1) to Fig. 2(b3-1). Here, the result is independent of the selected functional groups.

Mechanical properties of heterogeneous membranes

The cooperative effects of deformation and compaction resistance explain the mechanical properties of heterogeneous membranes, which can effectively alleviate both horizontal and vertical stresses. Tensile tests were performed to simulate the horizontal stresses on the membrane (Supplementary Fig. 20). The sample was stretched to a fixed value, held for 15 s, and then recovered. This process was repeated twice. As shown in Fig. 3b, the average tension force from the PT-1 to PT-5 membranes gradually increased from 840 ± 20 to 2650 ± 20 mN. Specifically, the tension force of the PT-1, PT-2 and PT-3 membranes gradually decreases with increasing holding time, and parts of the crumpled morphology became smooth under a stretched state (Supplementary Fig. 21), indicating that the crumpled morphology is capable of releasing stress. Within one hundred cycles of stretch tests (Fig. 3a1-a6, Supplementary Fig. 22), no visible cracks or fragmentation of the PT-1 to PT-3 membranes were observed, whereas the PT-4 and PT-5 membranes exhibited obvious cracks after five cycles (Fig. 3a7–a10). These results reflect the deformation characteristics of the crumpled morphology, thus effectively avoiding membrane defects, which is also confirmed by the tensile tests shown in Supplementary Fig. 23. Gold nanoparticle retention tests were also conducted to visually analyse the deformation behaviour of the peaks, and the detailed process is shown in the Supplementary Information. As shown in Fig. 3e and Supplementary Fig.16, gold nanoparticles were used as the markers, accompanied by a high-speed gas flow to strike the membrane. The deformation effect of the peaks effectively releases compressive stress, which is verified by narrowing the peak width from d1 to d2 to d3 (Figs. 3f1–3f3 and 3f1-1– 3f3-1) from atmospheric pressure to high pressure.

AFM height images and their corresponding quantitative nanomechanical maps were used to simulate the vertical stresses on the membrane surface, original SEM cross-section images were shown in Fig.3c and Supplementary Figs 17, 18. Four parameters are shown in Fig. 3d: the indentation depth, which reflects the deformation space when the membrane is closely attached to the substrate (mPSf membrane); the crumpled distance, which reflects the crumpled density; the crumpled height, which indicates the fluctuation degree of the crumpled structure; and the Young’s modulus, which reflects the difficulty in deformation. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 44e, the average crumpled heights from the PT-1 to PT-5 membranes gradually decreased from 128.2 ± 3.2 to 95.1 ± 2.3 nm and then rapidly decreased to 3.3 ± 0.2 nm. This finding suggests the disappearance of the crumpled morphology. The increase in the crumpled distance increases from 12.1 ± 1.3 to 125.1 ± 3.3 nm, which demonstrates a decrease in the crumpled density. AFM mechanical phase diagrams verify the mechanical microphase separation (Fig. 3g), demonstrating that the Young’s modulus at the peaks (yellow domains) is lower than that at the valleys (purple domains). We further used the AFM mechanical mode to compare the peaks and valleys in detail. In Fig. 3h, the Young’s moduli at the peaks from the PT-1 to PT-3 membranes are lower than those at the valleys, reflecting a greater indentation depth at the peaks than at the valleys. The indentation depth changes with attached force on the AFM tip, but the calculated Young’s modulus is almost independent of attached force (Supplementary Figs.44a-c). However, the PT-4 and PT-5 membranes, which have relatively low Young’s moduli, are compressible. Specifically, the indentation depth at valleys is lower than that in homogeneous membranes (PT-4 and PT-5). This result shows the enhanced compression resistance because of microphase separation, which increases the distribution of rigid groups at the valleys.

Gas separation performance of heterogeneous membranes

The heterogeneous membrane demonstrated gas separation performance under operating pressure. In Fig. 4a, at a pressure of 1.0 MPa, the CO2 permeance increases from 2350 GPU to 2967 GPU from the PT-1 to PT-3 membranes and then rapidly decreases to 706 GPU (PT-5 membrane). However, the CO2/N2 selectivity decreases slowly and then rapidly from the PT-1 to the PT-3 to the PT-5 membranes. The PT-3 membrane exhibited the highest CO2 permeance and acceptable CO2/N2 selectivity. The gas separation performance of the mPSf membrane is almost independent of pressure, indicating that pressure has no effect on the performance of PT membranes (Supplementary Fig. 26). The CO2/N2 separation performance with pressure is shown in Supplementary Figs. 27 and 28, and the CO2 and N2 permeance tested with pure gas is shown in Supplementary Fig. 35. Both the CO2 permeance and CO2/N2 selectivity of the PT-1, PT-2 and PT-3 membranes decrease slightly at low pressure and remain constant at operation pressure, but those of the PT-4 and PT-5 membranes decrease rapidly. According to the pressure cycle measurements in Supplementary Fig. 29, the heterogeneous membrane shows the same performance during increased and decreased pressures. On the basis of the pressure stability tests in Supplementary Fig. 30, the membrane performance is unchanged under the same pressure within a certain time. The PT-3 membrane treated at 120 °C for 4 h to simulate the real temperature of the flue gases in Supplementary Fig. 31 shows the same performance as that at room temperature, whereas the performance of the PT-5 membrane greatly decreases. The stretch tests also revealed the performance stability of heterogeneous membranes at different tensile rates (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 32). Fig. 4c and Supplementary Table 4 compare the heterogeneous membranes in this study with other state-of-the-art membranes under 1.0 MPa reported in the literatures that demonstrate great advantages in terms of gas separation performance. Moreover, the PT-1, PT-2 and PT-3 membranes also exhibited CO2/CH4 and CH4/N2 separation abilities within 3.0 MPa (Supplementary Fig. 33). The CH4/N2 separation ability is attributed to a high CH4/N2 solubility selectivity, which was obtained through deconvoluting the CH4 and N2 permeability into solubility and diffusivity coefficients on the basis of the solution‒diffusion model (Supplementary Fig. 34, Table 2, Table 3). Meanwhile, within operation pressure (from 1.0 to 3.0 MPa), the crumpled structure still cannot be squeezed onto the mPSf membrane (Supplementary Fig.44d).

The rearrangement of functional groups at the peaks and valleys endows the crumpled membrane with independent and cooperative dual-function regions. These regions can improve the membrane performance through increased gas diffusion and increased pressure resistance. Gold nanoparticle retention tests (Supplementary Fig. 36) were conducted to provide visual evidence of the diffusion difference in the heterogeneous structure (Supplementary Figs. 37 to 39). We fabricated a homogeneous crumpled membrane (Supplementary Fig. 8f to 8f3) with a common L-L IP reaction to compare the gas transfer behaviour with that of a heterogeneous crumpled membrane at 1.0 MPa, and the results are shown in Fig. 4d and Fig. 4e. In this process, gases can pass through the membrane, whereas the gold nanoparticles remain on the surface. Moreover, the gold nanoparticles, which have the same charge as the PT membranes in Supplementary Table 5, cannot be adsorbed on the membrane surface. Hence, the retention of gold nanoparticles was used to judge the gas transfer rate. In Fig. 4e, the coverages of the gold nanoparticles at both the peaks and valleys of the heterogeneous membranes are greater than those of the homogeneous membranes within a fixed time, which demonstrates that the heterogeneous structure is critical for improving gas transfer. In this structure, more amide groups accumulate at the peaks, remarkably increasing the CO2 solubility and constructing rapid gas transfer channels, whereas the phenyl groups in valleys maintain a high free volume due to steric hindrance effects. This is beneficial for improving the gas diffusion ability, especially under operating pressure. The largest coverage rate of gold nanoparticles in the PT-3 membrane explains the highest CO2 permeance shown in Fig. 4a. The rapid decrease in the CO2/N2 selectivity of the PT-4 and PT-5 membranes is mainly attributed to the facilitated transport mechanism25-27.

Two-dimensional (2D) resistance models28 and COMSOL Multiphysics simulations were introduced to better understand the gas transport behaviour in heterogeneous structures. In the resistance model shown in the Supplementary Information, the relationship describing gas permeation through a polymer membrane via Fick’s law is mathematically equivalent to Ohm’s law, which describes current flow through a resistor. Hence, the gas permeation rate is inversely proportional to the gas transport resistance. In Supplementary Fig. 40, the resistances of the heterogeneous crumpled membrane (R1), homogeneous crumpled membrane (R2) and homogeneous smooth membrane (R3) were calculated as R=1/BiA (R, B and A represent the gas transport resistance, gas permeance and surface area, respectively), and the results are shown in Supplementary Table 6. The results show that with increasing operation pressure, the gas transport resistance of the homogeneous structure increases rapidly, whereas that of the heterogeneous structure increases slowly. The series resistance model29 was also introduced to analyze the heterogeneous crumpled structure compared with the counterparts. From Supplementary Fig. 41 and Table 7, the result shows that CO2 permeance of selective layer is obviously higher than corresponding composite membranes, which indicates the total resistance of the composite membrane is mainly decided by the selective layer. Meanwhile, the CO2 permeance of heterogeneous polyamide layers is remarkably higher than the homogeneous counterparts, indicating the heterogeneous structure endows polyamide with enhanced gas permeation ability. Moreover, the mPSf membrane, which has a low resistance compared with other membranes with PA layers, has almost no effect on the overall resistance. We also Numerical simulations of the gas diffusion rate on the membrane permeate side using COMSOL Multiphysics were conducted to analyse this process, and the calculation method is described in the Supplementary Information and Supplementary Fig. 42. In Fig. 4f, the gas diffusion rate through the peaks is significantly higher than that through the valleys. Similar to the results in Fig. 4e, the PT-3 membrane also has the highest gas diffusion rate, which is also attributed to the low crosslinking density compared with those of the PT-1 and PT-2 membranes (Supplementary Table 1). Furthermore, the heterogeneous structure can effectively avoid the production of stress concentration points between peaks and valleys (Supplementary Fig. 43), which is vital for decreasing the number of membrane defects, especially under consecutive stress effects.

To analyse the economic advantages of heterogeneous membranes for CO2 capture, a typical two-stage membrane process was simulated on the basis of the assumptions of our previous study30. The detailed calculation process and a comparison of all the membranes are shown in Supplementary Fig. 45 and Table 8. The CO2 capture energy consumption (Supplementary Fig. 45a) decreases with pressure and then increases, as explained in our previous report31. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 45b, the membrane area requirements decrease with pressure due to the increased driving force. Overall, the CO2 capture cost decreases with pressure (Supplementary Fig. 45c). The PT-3 membrane has a minimum CO2 capture cost of $26.2 per tonne of CO2 at 0.8 MPa, which shows good potential for CO2 capture.
paper_content.methods:
Preparation of the mPSf membrane

Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS, 0.25 g, 0.5 wt.%), dibutyltin dilaurate (DBD, 0.2 g, 0.4%) and tetraethyl orthosilicate (TEOS, 0.2 g, 0.4 wt.%) were dissolved in n-heptane and stirred at 35 °C for 30 min under humidified conditions, thus obtaining PDMS prepolymer solution. PDMS, DBD and TEOS were used as monomers, catalysts and crosslinking agents, respectively, in the crosslinking reaction. The PSf ultrafiltration support was immersed in sodium dodecyl sulphate (SDS, 0.5 wt%) solution to remove organic solvent retained in the membrane pores, followed by drying at 60 °C for 10 h. The treated PSf membrane was coated with a PDMS solution, with a preset wet coating thickness (the gap between the PSf support and coating knife) of 200 μm (gap accuracy ± 5 μm), whereas the thickness of the PDMS layer in the mPSf membrane was approximately 100 nm. The casting membranes were dried at 30 °C and 40% RH in an artificial climate chamber (Climacell 222R, Germany) for at least two hours. The treated PSf support was denoted as the modified PSf (mPSf) membrane.

Fabrication of heterogeneous crumpled membranes

The membrane was fabricated using a microzone interfacial polymerization (IP) process. The aqueous phase solution was fabricated with 0.1-0.3 wt% PIP and 0.1 wt% Na2CO3, and 0.1 wt% TMC dissolved in hexane was used as the organic phase solution. The amide groups formed using the IP reaction constitute the repeating units in the polymer segments of the crumpled membrane. The prepared solutions were sealed and stored in a water bath at 25 °C for 30 min to avoid solvent evaporation. First, the mPSf membrane, which was clamped between two Teflon frames, was immersed in 30 mL of TMC solution for 3 min. Then, the excess solution was removed. Then, the membrane was incubated for 30 s, 60 s, 120 s, 200 s and 240 s as the residence time. Then, the treated mPSf membrane was immediately soaked in 50 mL of PIP solution for 15 min. Subsequently, the resulting membrane was washed thoroughly with deionized water and dried at 30 °C and 40% RH for 12 h. The obtained heterogeneous membrane with a crumpled morphology was attached to the mPSf membrane, forming a selective layer of the membrane. The membranes fabricated with different residence times of 30 s, 60 s, 120 s, 200 s and 240 s were named the PT-1, PT-2, PT-3, PT-4 and PT-5 membranes, respectively. Among them, the PT-1, PT-2 and PT-3 membranes have heterogeneous structures with crumpled morphologies, whereas the PT-4 and PT-5 membranes are homogeneous with smooth morphologies.

Fabrication of homogeneous crumpled membranes

The membrane was fabricated via a common liquid‒liquid interfacial polymerization process. The aqueous phase solution was fabricated with 0.1 wt% PIP and 0.1 wt% Na2CO3 (A solution), and 0.1 wt% TMC dissolved in hexane (B solution) was used as the organic phase solution. The prepared solutions were sealed and stored in a water bath at 25 °C for 30 min to avoid solvent evaporation. First, 50 mL of A solution was poured into the beaker, and then 50 mL of B solution was slowly added and left for 15 min. A polyamide film was formed at the interface of the two phases, after which it was extracted with a substrate. The obtained homogeneous crumpled membrane, attached to a mPSf membrane, was used to compare the mixed-gas separation performance with heterogeneous counterpart. While, the resultant homogeneous crumpled membrane, attached to a PSf support, was used to compare the pure-gas selectivity with heterogeneous counterpart to judge the gas transfer mechanism. The resulting membrane was washed thoroughly with deionized water and dried at 30 °C and 40% RH for 12 h.

Characterizations of the membranes

The morphology of the membranes was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, nano-SEM 430, FEI, USA) and atomic force microscopy (AFM, Bruker, Dimension IconXR, Germany). AFM was also used to characterize the membrane surface morphology and obtain information, including indentation, crumpled height and crumpled distance. AFM-IR (Bruker, Anasys nanoIR3s, Germany) nanoinfrared spectroscopy was used to perform microzone chemical analysis to characterize the microphase separation of the functional groups. Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy of the membranes in the wavenumber range of 400 cm−1 to 4000 cm−1 was performed using an FTS-6000 instrument (Bio-Rad, USA). X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALAB 250Xi, Thermo Fischer, USA) was used to characterize the element composition and degree of crosslinking of the crumpled membrane with Al Kα radiation. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (2θ=10° to 50°) was performed at room temperature with a Bruker-AXS D8 diffractometer with a Cu Kα (λ=1.54 Å) radiation detector. Raman spectroscopy (Renishaw, inVia Qontor, Britain) was used to analyse the TMC distribution in the swollen PDMS layer and the C=O, C=C, C-H and C-N groups in the membrane. A Raman scanning model, which is based on different functional groups, was used to demonstrate the formation process of peaks and valleys in the crumpled structure. Gold nanoparticle retention tests were conducted to provide visual evidence of the difference in gas diffusion between the peaks and valleys of the heterogeneous structure, and the detailed testing process is described in the Supplementary Information. N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms of the swelling PDMS layer were performed on BSD-660M (Beishide Instrument, China) at 77 K, and the pore size distribution of the PDMS layer was calculated based on the Barrett-Joyner-Halenda (BJH) model. The swelling PDMS layer was peeled off the mPSf membrane by immersing into N, N-dimethylformamide (DMF) to eliminate the influence of PSf substrate on the analysis of pore size. Subsequently, the PDMS layer was rinsed with ethanol and vacuum degassed at 25 ℃ for 10 h to remove the residual solvent before testing.

Mechanical property measurement

The membrane was cut into a square of 1 cm × 1 cm, and the effect of vertical force was tested by atomic force microscopy (AFM, Bruker, Dimension IconXR, Germany). The effect of horizontal stretch tension was tested using a mechanical test module in an AES-4SD flexible electronic device comprehensive test platform with different stretch rates. The mechanical properties, including the Young’s modulus, were gauged using peak force quantitative nanomechanical mapping (PF-QNM) imaging via AFM. The RTESPA-525-30 was used as the AFM tip to conduct the PF-QNM experiment, which is composed of 0.01-0.025 Ωcm Antimony (n)-doped Si with an aluminium reflective coating on the backside of the cantilever. The tip and cantilever parameters are presented below. The tip parameters included a tip height of 10-15 μm and an end curvature radius of 30 nm; the cantilever parameters included a cantilever thickness of 5.75 μm, a cantilever length of 125 μm, a cantilever width of 40 μm, a cantilever frequency of 525 kHz, and a spring constant of 200 N/m. The selected tip with a large spring constant of 200 N/m has a hardness property that is beneficial for rapid scanning. Moreover, the cantilever is difficult to deform and can truly reflect the indentation depth. A selected tip with a high resonance frequency of 525 kHz quickly reaches the equilibrium state. Thus, for the crumpled structure with a large undulation, the morphology can be rapidly detected. This is consistent with the SEM results, indicating that the crumpled structure is close to the PSf support. A selected tip with a curvature radius of 30 nm can avoid damage to the ultrathin sample surface caused by the contact between the tip side and the sample. In this work, the applied force on the membrane surface via AFM tips converted to the gas pressure is large enough to squeeze the peaks tightly on the mPSf surface, and the testing process was shown in Supplementary Fig.44. Hence, the tested Young's modulus of the peak, similar to the valley, was also obtained via pressing the peaks tightly on the mPSf support, which can eliminate the influence of morphology on the test results. Before and after performing each test, the deflection sensitivity calibration was performed on a sapphire sample that was assumed to have a less than 5% error. Meanwhile, the tip radius was calibrated using a standard highly oriented pyrolytic graphite film (18 GPa). This calibrated tip radius (35 ± 3 nm), which accounts for tip blunting, was used for all subsequent contact area calculation and modulus extractions from our samples.

Gas permselectivity test

The gas permselectivity of the membranes was tested with custom-made testing equipment27. The feed gas passed through a humidifier at 35 °C and a dehumidifier at ambient temperature successively so that the feed gas was saturated with water vapour before it entered the test unit. Thus, in this study, the humidified conditions were 100% relative humidity. The structure of the membrane cell is shown in Supplementary Fig. 24. The detailed gas permeance (R) is expressed in units of GPU, and the CO2/N2 (CH4) selectivity equals the CO2 permeance divided by the N2 (CH4) permeance.

The permeance is calculated via Eq. (1) as follows:

R = Qi / (A⋅ΔPi) (1)

where Q represents the permeate flow rate through the membrane, A is the effective membrane area, and ΔP is the partial pressure difference between the upstream and downstream sides of the membrane. A was calculated using the following two methods because of the crumpled morphology with different membrane surfaces. One is the real area obtained from the AFM results in Supplementary Fig. 25, and the other is the fixed area of the membrane cell. In the main text, all the performances were calculated with real areas.

The single-gas permeabilities P (Barrer) of the crumpled membranes were evaluated using a Labthink VAC-V2(EX) apparatus based on the constant volume/variable-pressure method. In this work, we utilized the stacked PA layers, with a thickness of about 50 μm to perform the time-lag measurements, which can effectively eliminate the impact of porous support. The PA layer was delaminated from the composite membrane by immersing it in n-hexane to remove the mPSf support, which will not damage the PA layer. The peeled PA layer with a surface area of 30 cm2 should be carefully transferred with a glass plate, then this process was repeated to accumulate more PA layers. The stacked PA layers were treated at 120 ℃ in a vacuum and then compressed at 3.0 MPa before testing to remove the residual solvent. To reduce the workload, after collecting some PA layers, we folded them several times to increase the effective thickness. The measurement was carried out on circular membrane samples fabricated by masking with adhesive aluminium foil with an effective exposed area of 3.14 cm2. The diffusivity coefficient D (cm2 s−1) was calculated using the time lag method as expressed in Eq. (2):

D = l^2 / (6θ) (2)

where l is the membrane thickness and θ is the time lag of the permeability measurement.

The solubility coefficient S (cm3 (STP) cm−3 cmHg−1) was calculated from the ratio of the gas permeability coefficient to the diffusivity coefficient using Eq. (3) as follows:

S = P / D (3)

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Comments on the manuscript NCOMMS-25-15480
This manuscript presents an experimental study on the preparation and characterization of membranes, focuses on the
development of advanced polymer membranes for gas separation aiming to simultaneously enhance separation
performance and structural robustness. The authors introduce a novel “micro-zone interfacial polymerization” technique to
reconstruct the polymer network, yielding a “heterogeneous, crumpled morphology”. This structure exhibits microphase
separation, where the “peak regions”, enriched with amide groups, function as fast CO₂ transport channels and, on the other
hand, the “valley regions”, containing more rigid phenyl groups, contribute to improved CO₂ diffusion and pressure-induced
compaction resistance. The cooperative effect of these dual-function zones significantly enhances mechanical resilience
and gas separation efficiency.
The topic is interesting but the manuscript presents a series of weaknesses and some aspects that should be clarified.
Among them are following:
1) Please consider having a professional English editor review the document before final submission.
2) Throughout the manuscript, the authors discuss the application of their membranes for high-pressure gas separation.
However, most of the experiments are performed at 1.0 MPa, which can hardly be considered high pressure in the field of
gas separation. High pressures could be in the range of 80-150 bar, so the manuscript could mislead.
3) The abstract in its current format seems too long (lines 10 to 61). Perhaps this text could be divided into an abstract with
the main ideas and another section serving as an introduction.
4) The meaning of some expressions is not entirely clear. What do the authors mean by "structural ability" (line 40)? What do
the authors mean by "gas diffusion ability" (line 45)? The same goes for "dense micropores" (line 67).
5) Lines 330-332, the authors write: “The treated PSf membrane was coated with PDMS solution, using a pre-set wet coating
thickness (the gap between the support and coating knife) of 200 μm”. Does this mean that the mPSf membrane has a dense
PDMS layer of around 200 μm?
6) The role of each of the materials used in the preparation of the membranes (PDMS, TEOS, DBD, TMC, PIP) should be
more clearly identified, whether in the structure of the membrane or in its functionalization.
7) Some abbreviations are used in the main body of the manuscript and are only defined in the supplementary material (e.g.,
PIP).
8) Regarding gas permselectivity tests: The manuscript should explain why the feed gas mixture must have 100% relative
humidity. How much water permeates through the membrane? Working with moisture-saturated gas streams can be
problematic in industrial operations.
9) The format of references should be carefully reviewed. For example, the authors' names in references 1 and 3.
10) Supplementary information (page 18), Figures S20 (a) and (b). Can the decrease in CO2 permeance with pressure be
attributed to a facilitated transport mechanism?
11) Supplementary information (page 34). The assumed price for the membrane module ($50/m2) is very low. There are
many reliable references that show much higher prices. For example, Baker (IEChR 47, 2008, 2109) and Lin et al (JMS 493
(2015) 794) report that “The membrane skid has an estimated installed cost of $500/m2 membrane area, which includes
membrane modules, module housings, valves, instrumentation, piping and frame structures”. Therefore, I suggest that the

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Wang et al. reported an interfacial polymerization strategy to create a heterogeneous crumpled polymer membrane with
microphase separation. The authors claimed that the dual-functional regions enhanced the CO2 transport and structural
robustness. Overall, this paper is interesting but the quality of current version is far from satisfactory. More solid evidence is
need to clarify whether the heterogeneity is on the surface or in the bulk film. The formation mechanism of such wrinkled
structure with heterogeneous composition also requires further investigation. In addition, the following issues should be
properly addressed after major revision.
Direct evidence from compositional characterization is needed to support the claim that “the heterogeneous structure with a
discovered microphase separation”. AFM-IR may only reveal the surface composition rather than the bulk composition of the
film. Rearrangement of functional groups towards the surface or a complete contrast of bulk composition in the microscale
regions needs to be clarified. ToF-SIMS depth profiling maybe helpful for such analysis.
The schematic in Fig S1 is misleading. I don’t think there are such micro-trench structures formed in the PDMS in the first
step of TMC soaking and evaporation. More evidence is needed to show if there are such “micro-zones” in the PDMS, if the
authors would like to define the IP synthesis in this way. Fig. S4 suggest that the pore structures are connected rather than
individual channels, which contradicts to the schematic in Fig S1. The resolution of Fig S4 is also very low. Cross-sectional
TEM with high-resolution EDX mapping could provide more detailed information about TMC distribution in PDMS, which is
critical for understanding this IP synthesis.
In Fig. 1, why does the weight of PDMS decrease with increased residence time of swelling PDMS layer? Shouldn’t there be
more TMC loaded into the polymer matrix with longer soaking time?
The crumpled morphology observed in PT-1, PT-2, and PT-3 closely resembles Turing patterns, and previous studies have
reported Turing structures in polyimide membranes (Science, 360, 518-521 (2018)). Can the authors clarify whether the
formation of such crumpled morphology in PT-1, PT-2, and PT-3 can be explained by the reaction-diffusion theory?
The authors stated that “Young’s modulus at peaks from PT-1 to PT-3 membranes are lower than that at valleys.” Could this
be attributed to the proximity of the valleys to the substrate and the overall thin nature of the membrane, leading to a
significant substrate effect? How do the authors account for and minimize such substrate-induced artifacts in modulus
measurement? The indentation depth of less than 10 nm for the valley in Fig. 3h is also problematic as surface effect may
become dominant.
Fig. 3b and Fig. S15: Conducting tensile tests on membranes with a supporting substrate may not accurately reflect the
mechanical properties of the crumpled film. Stress–strain curves are needed to better interpret the mechanical properties.
The authors stated that “The largest coverage rate of gold nanoparticles in the PT-3 membrane explains the highest CO2
permeance in Fig.4a.” So do PT-1 to PT-3 exhibit higher surface area than PT-4 to PT-5? Could the authors quantify this
difference in surface area and examine whether the magnitude of increase correlates with the observed enhancement in gas
permeance? A direct comparison would provide better insight into the structure-property relationship.
The schematic in Scheme S1 indicates that both humidifier and dehumidifier are placed before the test cell. However, if the
goal is to measure CO2/N2 separation under 100% relative humidity conditions, why is the dehumidifier positioned before
the test cell rather than before gas chromatography (GC) to protect it? Additionally, “Sweep” in Scheme S2 was mistakenly
written as “Sweap”.
While Figure S24 presents the trend in CO2 permeance, the corresponding variation in CO2/N2 selectivity is not explicitly
discussed. Could the authors provide the data and analyze whether selectivity follows a similar or distinct trend?
Figure S25 shows a decrease in both CO2 permeance and selectivity between 0.1-1MPa, followed by an increase in
permeance and a decrease in selectivity beyond 1.0 MPa. Could the authors elaborate on the underlying mechanisms
responsible for this observation?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript describes the preparation, characterization and separation performance of polyamide membranes made by
controlled interfacial polymerization between a swollen PDMS film with acyl chloride in contact with an aqueous diamine
solution. This procedure yields highly permeable and selective membranes with a wrinkled surface morphology. The
separation performance is discussed in correlation with the membrane morphology and microstructure. The results are
supported by a range of different morphological, compositional and mechanical studies, as well as computational methods.
The gas separation performance is excellent, above the state of the art, with high permeance and high selectivity.
Overall the work is done well and the results are convincing and occasionally exceed the state of the art. Nevertheless, not
all results and points in the discussion are completely clear.
These points need to be improved before it may become suitable for publication. Some specific remarks that require a
revision of the manuscript are given below:
The relatively high permeance of the membranes can at least in part be ascribed to the roughness of the surface, and thus to
the effective increase in the surface area. A similar approach has already been applied by the group of Matthias Wessling to
enhance mass transport in hollow fibres (e.g. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.memsci.2005.02.022,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.memsci.2009.10.003). This must be discussed in the state of the art.
Evident errors:
CO2 permeance (ca. 2000 for PT1, Fig S25A) and CH4 permeance (ca. 1200 for PT-1, Fig S25C) does not lead to a
CO2/CH4 selectivity of almost 10 but to less than 2! Apparently there is an evident error in some of the measurements or
calculations, which should be checked and where necessary corrected throughout the manuscript.
Specific points:
The manuscript claims to have produced a micro-phase separated membrane with the peaks composed of more amide
groups and the valleys with more phenyl groups (line 57-58). Since the amide groups are covalently bonded to the phenyl
groups of TMC, this statement must be further explained. The only way to change the ratio of amide groups and phenyl
groups is by a different cross-link density or by the formation of free carboxylic acid groups instead of amide groups from the
reaction of the corresponding acyl chloride with water instead of amine. In this sense, the cross-link density is likely more
important than the composition as such. Also, the confinement of the PDMS is fundamental for the transport properties and
should be discussed more accurately. Does the interfacial polymerization also penetrate within the PDMS layer? PDMS
itself has a CO2/N2 selectivity equal to ca. 11-12 (-). The very strong positive deviation from this value indicates that the
PDMS is no longer the main resistance in the film.
Figure S1 is not completely clear and should also show the PSF support. Besides the top surface images, also the cross
sections of the membranes should be shown, indicating clearly the thickness of each active layer. In this light, the sampling
depth of IR is typically a few micrometers. Therefore, the analysis shows not only the active layer but also the support and/or
the top-layer, which may lead to erroneous conclusions related to presumed microphase separation. Please discuss in more
detail.
Figure S25 (SI line 340) shows unlikely high selectivity CH4/N2. Since CH4 is larger than N2, diffusion selectivity is strongly
in favour of N2 (e.g. Teplyakov and Meares, doi: 10.1016/0950-4214(90)80030-O), and the selectivity must apparently be
based on solubility selectivity. Is there any evidence for this? Please discuss.
Fig S30 caption “…is based on the difference of Young's modulus between the peaks and valleys”: Is there indeed any proof
for the differences in modulus? How can the authors exclude that indentation of the peaks is easier because of empty space
below the peaks, whereas the valleys rest on the support and need to be compressed rather than just bent? Please discuss
the mechanical properties also in terms of morphology and not only in terms of microstructure.
Fig. S24: The increase in permeance is ascribed to the appearance of defects in samples PT-4 and PT-5. However, both
samples have a lower permeance than the samples PT-1, 2 and 3. Defects would first of all increase the permeance of the
slowest species.
The authors should specify in the experimental part what kind of tip is used for the AFM analysis and what this means for the
analysis of the results.
Especially in non-homogeneous microphase separated polymers, the tip size, type and cantilever properties are crucial for
the result that should be expected and should therefore be mentioned (see for instance M. Longo, et al., Polymer, 156 (2018)
22–29. doi:10.1016/j.polymer.2018.09.043.
In this light, the conclusion in line 189-191 that Young’s modulus in the peaks is lower than that in the valleys may not be
correct. The deformation measured in the peaks reflect both the indentation and the deformation of the entire thin film,
whereas the deformation in the valleys reflects only the indentation.
Gold nanoparticles are dispersed in the feed and the deposition on the surface is discussed as presumed evidence of the
high low rate of the gas across the membrane. However, the dimensions of the nanoparticles are said to be 5 nm, whereas
the smallest scale bar in Fig S27 is 200 nm. Thus, the particles are not visible at this scale. Figure d1-1 and d2-1 show an
irregular morphology with small depressions between thin ‘walls’. The changes seen from figure d1 to d1-1 and d2 to d2-1
are a different surface morphology with features up to 50 nm and do not represent the 5 nm nanoparticles.
Furthermore, what is the linear perpendicular flow velocity of the gas on the membrane? Is this sufficient to overcome gravity
and act as the main driving force for particle transport, rather than gravity or electrostatic interactions?
Overall, the proof of the gas flow profile through the membrane, with preference for the higher areas, seems insufficient on
the one hand, but perhaps not particularly relevant on the other hand. Proof of the collocation of the particles on the tops and
not on the valleys of the crumpled membrane surface requires the demonstration of the cross-sectional image of the
membrane, appropriately made by embedding the surface in a resin (without moving the nanoparticles) and subsequent
TEM analysis of s thin slice of this sample.
The transport model in Figure S28 does not have a strong scientific basis. The origin of the coefficients 2 and 3 is unclear
and should be justified quantitatively. Instead, it makes more sense to express the transport in terms of ‘true’ effective surface
area and effective membrane thickness (of the effective dense skin). The role of the individual components (PDMS and
polyamide) should also be discussed in terms of more common models such as mixed matrix or resistances in series.
Line 246-247: please explain what is meant with “The cooperative effects of functional groups rearrangement at peaks and
valleys, explain the heterogeneous membranes with excellent gas separation performance”.
Commercial membranes for gas separation are normally produced by a continuous process and are often formed by hollow
fibres as well as flat sheet membranes. A brief discussion on the feasibility of continuous production and the possible use of
hollow fibre configuration should be added.
Minor issues:
Fig. S7: the text in the IR spectra is too small to identify the peaks.
English language needs radical improvement.
The article is sometimes difficult to follow because of repetitions and not always logical order of the data and the discussion.
Overall conclusion:
The manuscript may be suitable for publication, but the obvious mistakes must be corrected and all weaknesses should be
improved or properly justified. This will require a major revision of the present manuscript.

General reply: We thank the reviewer for noting the novelty and the significance of our

Reply: In this work, the thickness of crumpled layer is about 60 nm (Supplementary
Fig. 19). Hence, AFM-IR characterization, with a sampling depth of several
micrometers, can reveal the bulk composition of the crumpled layer rather than only
surface composition. The AFM-IR technology combines a high nanoscale resolution
with a high chemical sensitivity of infrared spectroscopy. The microscopic morphology
information of the surface was obtained via AFM by touching the sample surface via
the probe, which cannot damage the samples. While, the infrared spectrum detects the
thermal expansion signals of the samples and converts into the infrared absorption
spectrum in the micro-area. This combination enables AFM-IR to identify and image
the chemical composition of materials at the nanoscale, which has been widely adopted
and recognized for identifying subtle structural differences within the nanoscale
(Nature, 2023, 620, 545-551; Nat. Mater. 2023, 22, 873-879; Nat. Commun. 2023, 14,
3941). Hence, in this work, AFM-IR characterization can fully reflect the composition
differences at peaks and valleys in the crumpled structure.
The strength of ToF-SIMS lies in its high accuracy and capability for atomic-layer
thickness detection; however, its limitation is a low microstructure resolution. Although
theoretical resolution can reach as low as 100 nm provided from the instrument
manufacturer, recent reports demonstrate that the practical resolution remains at the
micrometer scale (Nature, 2024, 632, 528-535; Nature, 2024, 628, 299-305; Nat.
Energy 2023, 8, 934-945; Nat. Commun. 2024, 15, 7516). In my work, the maximum
distance between peak and valley in the crumpled structure is about 50 nm. We also
conducted TOF-SIMs characterizations with different instruments (IONTOF, TOF.
SIMS 5, Germany; ULVAC-PHI, PHI nanoTOF 3+, Japan), but it was difficult to
distinguish the peak and valley locations in the crumpled structures.

would like to define the IP synthesis in this way.

4. The crumpled morphology observed in PT-1, PT-2, and PT-3 closely resembles
Turing patterns, and previous studies have reported Turing structures in polyimide
membranes (Science, 360, 518-521 (2018)). Can the authors clarify whether the
formation of such crumpled morphology in PT-1, PT-2, and PT-3 can be explained by
the reaction-diffusion theory?
Reply: In this work, we synthesized a polyamide membrane with a crumpled
morphology, which is similar to Turing structure to some extent. However, our work
aims at constructing heterogeneous structure at peaks and valleys within polymer
membranes for gas separation under high pressure. Although they still exhibit crumpled
morphology, for the purpose of avoiding controversy, we do not conduct in-depth
analysis to judge whether they belong to the Turing structure.
Currently, since the first publication of the Turing membrane (Science, 2018, 360, 518),
extensive researches on Turing structures, with new construction mechanisms, were
conducted in the membranes (Science, 2024, 385, 647; Sci. Adv. 2024, 10, eadr9260;
Angew. Chem. Int. Ed. 2025, 64, e202503090), greatly promoting the influence of
Turing structure in separation membranes.
Both our work and Zhang’s work (Science, 2018, 360, 518) fabricated polymer
membrane via interfacial polymerization (IP) reaction, which can be explained by the
reaction-diffusion theory. However, the formation mechanism of the crumpled
morphology (similar to the Turing structure) in our work is different with that in
Zhang’s work. 1. We constructed micropores (microzones) in the intermediate layer
(PDMS) with a swelling method, as the IP reaction sites, to enrich organic phase
monomers (TMC). Variations in IP reaction rates between the micropores and PDMS
surface result in the formation of a crumpled structure; 2. We constructed peaks and
valleys in the crumpled morphology with heterogeneous structures to enable the peaks
and valleys with individual values at structural stability and gas transfer respectively.
In terms of structure, peaks can effectively relieve external stresses through
deformation behavior; while the valleys, composed of more rigid groups, enhance the
compactness resistance to maintain a high free volume. In terms of gas transfer, peaks
with more amides form CO -philic channels which increase the CO permeation, while
2 2
the valleys maintain high CO diffusion ability. The cooperative effects of dual-function
2
regions in polymer membrane enhance the separation ability and structural stability
simultaneously; 3. The heterogeneous crumpled membrane provided a 300% increase
in CO permeance and CO /N selectivity compared to homogeneous counterparts,
2 2 2
which also achieved one order of magnitude higher than that of state-of-the-art
membranes under real operation pressure. Meanwhile, the heterogeneous membrane
also shows excellent CO /CH separation performance.
2 4
5.1 The authors stated that “Young’s modulus at peaks from PT-1 to PT-3 membranes
are lower than that at valleys.” Could this be attributed to the proximity of the valleys
to the substrate and the overall thin nature of the membrane, leading to a significant
substrate effect?
Reply: We’re very sorry for this misunderstanding caused by the unclear description of
Young’s modulus testing methods. In this work, the applied force on the membrane

This manuscript describes the preparation, characterization and separation performance

swollen PDMS film with acyl chloride in contact with an aqueous diamine solution.
This procedure yields highly permeable and selective membranes with a wrinkled
surface morphology. The separation performance is discussed in correlation with the
membrane morphology and microstructure. The results are supported by a range of
different morphological, compositional and mechanical studies, as well as
computational methods. The gas separation performance is excellent, above the state of
the art, with high permeance and high selectivity.

completely clear.

origin of the coefficients 2 and 3 is unclear and should be justified quantitatively.

transport model. Commonly, the gas transport resistance is inversely proportional to
the gas permeation. In our work, the gas permeability reflects the overall performance
of the PT membrane, so the gas transport resistance also reflects the resistance of the
entire structure and should not be divided into the resistance of peaks and valleys
respectively. The gas transport resistance of membranes is calculated as follow.
According to Tripodi’s report (J Membrane Sci., 1981, 8, 233-246), the gas transport
resistance can be calculated as follow. The permeation rate, or flux, for component i
through a polymeric membrane can be described by:
Q = P AΔc/l= BAΔc (1)
i i i i i i i i
where Qi is the permeation rate of component i, P is the intrinsic permeability of the
i
polymeric membrane to component i, B is the permeance of the polymeric membrane
i
to component i, A is the surface area of membrane, 1 is the membrane thickness, Δc
i i i
is the concentration difference of component i across the membrane (in the case of gas
permeation, this is the partial pressure difference). Using the electrical analog, the
above relationship describing permeation through a polymer membrane is
mathematically equivalent to Ohm’s law which describes current flow through a
resistor:
I = E/R (2)
Conceptually the current, I, can be equated with the permeation rate, Q. The driving
force for current flow, (i.e. the difference in electric potential E), is analogous to the
concentration gradient Δc. Hence, we can define, then, a resistance to permeate flow,
i
R, which is equivalent to the electrical resistance R:
i
R = l/PA=1/BA (3)
i i i i i
so that combining (1) and (3)
Qi = Δc/R (4)
i i
Based on equation (3) and schematic diagram shown in Supplementary Fig. 38, the gas
transport resistance of all the membranes is decided by the membrane thickness, surface
area and gas permeability. In Supplementary Table 5, the results of R show that with
i
the increase of operation pressure, the gas transport resistance of the homogeneous
structure increases rapidly, while that of the heterogeneous structure grows slowly,
which further indicates the heterogeneous structure with a strong pressure-resistance.
The modifications are shown in line 303-316 in the main text, Supplementary Fig. 38,
Table 5 in revised Supplementary Information with yellow highlight.
14.2 The role of the individual components (PDMS and polyamide) should also be
discussed in terms of more common models such as mixed matrix or resistances in series.
Reply: In the resistance model of membrane permeation (J Membrane Sci., 1981, 8,
233-246), the total resistance is a function of the resistance in each layers including PA
layer, mPSf membrane. Meanwhile, the mPSf membrane, with a low resistance
compared with other membranes with PA layers, shows almost no effect on the overall
resistance. Therefore, the resistance of the PT membrane is mainly concentrated in the
PA layer.
15. Line 246-247: please explain what is meant with “The cooperative effects of
functional groups rearrangement at peaks and valleys, explain the heterogeneous
membranes with excellent gas separation performance”.
Reply: We modified this sentence as “The rearrangement of functional groups at peaks
and valleys endow the crumpled membrane with independent and cooperative dual-
function regions, which can improve the membrane performance from increased gas
diffusion and enhanced pressure resistance”.
In terms of gas diffusion, more amide groups are accumulated at peaks, remarkably
increasing the CO solubility and constructing rapid gas transfer channels; While the
2
phenyl groups in valleys maintain a high free volume due to the steric hindrance effects,
which is beneficial to improving gas diffusion ability especially under high pressure.
From the perspective of mechanical robustness, the cooperative effects of deformation
at peaks and compaction-resistance ability at valleys, explain the heterogeneous
membrane with excellent mechanical property, which can effectively alleviate both the
horizontal and vertical stresses with stable structure and is critical to achieve high-
pressure separation. The modifications are shown in line 276-279 in revised main text.
16. Commercial membranes for gas separation are normally produced by a continuous
process and are often formed by hollow fibers as well as flat sheet membranes. A brief
discussion on the feasibility of continuous production and the possible use of hollow
fiber configuration should be added.
Reply: We thank for your positive suggestion. In this work, the microzone interfacial
polymerization technology shows no special requirements for the membrane shape. For
hollow fiber membranes, our design is to cover the hollow fiber membrane with a
PDMS layer via a dip-coating technology at first, followed by immersing into one
monomer solution to construct micro areas, and then react with another monomer
solution to conduct interfacial polymerization reactions. Thus, a heterogeneous
crumpled membrane can be constructed on the outside of the hollow fiber membrane.
If the PDMS layer is coated on the inside of the hollow fibers, the heterogeneous
structure can also be obtained.
Minor issues:

Reply: We have increased the font size of the texts in Supplementary Fig. 9 (original
Fig. 7).

order of the data and the discussion.
Reply: The language has been polished by a professional English editing policy, and
we further improved the logic of this manuscript in depth.
Overall conclusion:
The manuscript may be suitable for publication, but the obvious mistakes must be
corrected and all weaknesses should be improved or properly justified. This will require
a major revision of the present manuscript.
Reply: We sincerely appreciate this reviewer for praising comments and detailed
suggestions regarding the improvement of our manuscript.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors answered all the questions and changed the manuscript accordingly. Therefore, I think that the manuscript can be accepted for publication.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The experimental details are needed for determining the pore size in the PDMS layer. What instrument did the authors use to obtain Fig. S5? I cannot find any information in the experimental section.
The Raman depth profiling is also questionable. As far as I know, In confocal Raman imaging, the spatial resolution is typically about 200–500 nm, depending on the excitation wavelength and the numerical aperture (NA) of the objective lens. How could the authors obtain images with sub-100 nm resolution?
The authors still have not explained why TMC soaking led to pore formation in PDMS. Why did longer TMC soaking result in “damages the integrity of membrane structure”? Does this mean more pore structures formed or degradation to the PDMS polymer?
The authors did not understand my question about nanoindentation. What are the film thickness of the crumpled film at the valleys? If the film thickness at the valley is very small, the measurements are significantly affected by the substrate, which is widely acknowledged as the “substrate effect”. The other thing that the authors need to be aware of is that the tip radius is typically 20–100 nm. That means at indentation depths <10 nm, the measured response is dominated by the blunted tip apex rather than the designed geometry. This affects the contact area calculation which often leads to errors in hardness and modulus extraction. This is known as the “surface effect”.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors made a great effort correct any shortcomings and to improve the quality of the manuscript in general.
Only few points for discussion remain:
The title seems to be inverted: Gas separation with Binary-cooperative heterogeneous membranes sounds more
reasonable..
Response #3 point 5: Equation (1) is incorrect and must be D=l2/6Θ instead of D=l/6Θ2
Also the results do not seem to be correct. With a diffusion coefficient in the order of 10-5 cm2/s PDMS has a measurable time lag for a slab with a thickness of I mm. A film thickness of 100 micrometres would already be in the order of few seconds and membranes of 10 micrometers or less than 1 micrometre become unmeasurable short. Thus, if the authors have measured a measurable time lag, then this must have included the contribution of the porous support.
The authors made a great effort correct any shortcomings and to improve the quality of the manuscript in general. However, in some cases this opens new questions rather than answering the original questions. In other cases, the response is not satisfactory. Details are given below:
1) The title seems to be inverted: Gas separation with Binary-cooperative heterogeneous membranes sounds more
reasonable than Binary-cooperative heterogeneous membranes with gas separation.
2) The authors have performed time lag measurements to determine the gas diffusion coefficient and indirectly the solubility
of the gases (Response #3 point 5). However, equation (1) is incorrect and must be D=l2/6Θ instead of D=l/6Θ2. If they used
indeed this equation, then all calculations are wrong and must be repeated with the correct equation.
Secondly, regardless the equation used, time lag measurements seem impossible for the thin film membranes discussed in
this work. For instance, with a diffusion coefficient in the order of 10-5 cm2/s PDMS has a measurable time lag for a slab with
high thickness: a rapid calculation reveals that a film thickness of 100 micrometres would already give a time lag in the order
of few seconds. Instead, membranes of 100 nm, as reported in line 369 become unmeasurably short. Regarding the other
materials, polysulfone and polyamide, both have such a low permeability that the permeance can be high only if a very thin
film is obtained, and in this case the equation Θ=l2/6D leads again to unmeasurably short time lags.
Thus, the authors should report at least one representative original time lag measurement curve (permeate pressure vs
time). Thus, if the authors have measured a measurable time lag, then this must have included the contribution of the porous
support. In any case, their equation (1) is wrong, and thus most likely also their calculations. Therefore, all calculations
should be checked, and some original time lag curves should be reported in the supplementary information to allow the
reader to check the calculations and see if there are any anomalies in the original curves.
3) What is the instrumental time lag of the measurement setup? How fast can valves be opened and how quickly can the
pressure be read?
As a test for the linearity of the time lag, I suggest calibrating the setup with neat PDMS films of 50, 100, 200 and 500
micrometres and plotting the time lag as a function of l2, extrapolating to l=0 to determine the instrumental time lag (see e.g.
Fig 4 and Fig. 8 in https://doi.org/10.1016/j.memsci.2018.04.029)
4) The discussion on the mechanical tests remains unclear. The morphology has peaks and valleys but the force used in the
mechanical tests is so high that it is supposed to squeeze the peaks onto the harder porous membrane support. Although
the authors attribute the difference in hardness between peaks and valleys to microphase separation it cannot be excluded
that it is simply a matter of thickness of the softer coating layer.
According to line 230-231, the authors now calculate the indentation depths at the peaks by 230 subtracting the
corresponding crumpled heights in Fig. 3d. This is not fully clear. In any case it suggests that the samples are subjected to
much larger deformations than licit for indentation measurements. Measurements of Young’s modulus should be carried out
at low deformation in the elastic regime, not in the plastic regime. If it is necessary to press the thin layer of the crumpled
membrane onto the support before measuring its modulus, the measurement is clearly affected by the support, and thus not
representative for the film itself.
5) In line 297-299 the authors state: “The rapid decrease in the CO2/N2 297 selectivity of the PT-4 and PT-5 membranes is
attributed to the decreased free volume in the polymer network under pressure, which limits the solubility of gas molecules”.
This claim is in contrast with the results of the mechanical tests. Young’s modulus of these samples is in the order of GPa,
whereas the permeability measurements are carried out up to few MPa. It is more likely that pressure-dependence is related
to the dual mode sorption mechanism, where the Langmuir sites are gradually saturated, but it is even more likely that the
pressure-dependence is a result of the ‘squeezing’ of the crumpled membrane onto the support (analogous to Fig. 3c).
Therefore, it is essential that the authors report also the pressure needed to compress the crumpled areas of the membrane
(See also the previous comment).
6) Figure S18 (right photo) demonstrates that the PDMS also penetrates deep into the PSf layer. Thus, the representation of
a distinct PA layer on top of a distinct PDMS layer on top of a distinct PSf layer as the authors show in all schematic images
is not completely correct. Which consequences does this have for the transport mechanism of these membranes?
7) A clear cross-sectional SEM image must also be reported in the manuscript instead of just schematic drawings. This is the
key feature of the manuscript and should not be reported only in the SI.
8) The authors overlook one important hypothesis regarding the high permeances of these membranes: The permeance of
thin film composite membranes is proportional to the surface porosity: the lower the surface porosity, the smaller the ‘active’
area is. This is the reason for the use of a highly permeable gutter layer in thin film composite gas separation membranes
with a low-permeable selective film. The present work appears to be rather similar to this situation, with PDMS coated onto
PSf as the gutter layer for the selective PA film. However, air is the most permeable of all gutter materials and it seems that
this is confirmed by crumpling of the PA layer, which makes the film much more permeable. On the other hand, this does not
explain, how a porous PA can provide selectivity, and it seems that this could only be possible if the PA film is sealed by
PDMS too. Nevertheless, the permeance is much higher than that reported for instance by Freeman et al.
(https://doi.org/10.1016/j.memsci.2020.118009) where the membrane is prepared in the reverse order and PDMS is coated
onto a PA reverse osmosis membrane and where the mechanism is explained on the basis of resistances in series/in
parallel as discussed by Henis and Tripodi (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0376-7388(00)82312-1).
9) Referring to the previous point: the authors should explain their results not only
phenomenologically, but also using well known transport models for hybrid materials, such as the already mentioned model
of Henis and Tripodi
(https://doi.org/10.1016/S0376-7388(00)82312-1), the model for polymer blends by Robeson
(http://dx.doi.org/10.1021/ie100153q), as well as the well-known Maxwell model.
10) Typical RO membranes made by phase inversion have very low surface porosities, as low as 5%. If the surface porosity.
If the surface porosity of the PA membrane plays a role, for instance when closing the pores by pressing the PA film onto the
support coating, then this has a much higher impact on the permeance than the surface area of the membrane (see Fig. S25
and response to question #1, reviewer #3). In addition to the above models, the authors should consider the accessible
pores in their discussion and the gutter layer principle.
Minor details:
Figure S3: d) reads TEM surface image but should probably be SEM surface image

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
General reply: We sincerely appreciate this reviewer for praising comments and
detailed suggestions regarding the improvement of our manuscript. The following
contents are our point-by-point responses to the concerns raised by the reviewer.
1. The experimental details are needed for determining the pore size in the PDMS layer.
What instrument did the authors use to obtain Fig. S5? I cannot find any information in
the experimental section.
Reply: Thanks for your comments. N adsorption-desorption isotherms of the swelling
the pore size distribution of the PDMS layer was calculated based on the Barrett-Joyner-
Halenda (BJH) model. The experimental details were shown in line 440-447 in Methods
in revised main text with yellow highlight.
2. The Raman depth profiling is also questionable. As far as I know, in confocal Raman
imaging, the spatial resolution is typically about 200–500 nm, depending on the
excitation wavelength and the numerical aperture (NA) of the objective lens. How could
the authors obtain images with sub-100 nm resolution?
Reply: Thanks for the insightful question. We fully agree and acknowledge that the
optical diffraction limit of our confocal Raman system (governed by the laser
wavelength λ and the numerical aperture (NA) of the objective) defines its ultimate
spatial resolution. For our configuration with a 532 nm laser and a NA of 1.4, the
theoretical spatial resolution is about 200-300 nm, and we cannot achieve direct optical
resolution below this limit.
However, the scale bar of 100 nm in Supplementary Fig.6a1 and a2 do not represent
the optical resolution. Instead, it indicates the sampling interval of the depth profiling.
To reconstruct a chemical profile, the sampling interval (in this case, 100 nm) should
be smaller than the optical resolution, which can effectively capture the shape of the
TMC concentration gradient. Meanwhile, it can be discovered that the axis width of
TMC signal areas in the Raman depth profiling is greater than that of an individual pore
channel on the PDMS layer, which is attributed to the scattering phenomenon of Raman
lasers, caused by the overlap of TMC signals adjacent to the channels. We have added
explanations about the scale bar in the Supplementary Fig.6 with yellow highlights.
3.1 The authors still have not explained why TMC soaking led to pore formation in
PDMS.
Reply: In this work, the solvent (n-hexane) in TMC solution, with similar solubility
parameter compared with PDMS, leads to the formation of pore structures in the PDMS
layer, which is explained by solvent-induced swelling mechanism and researched in
previous reports (J Membrane Sci., 2015, 475, 488). The detailed formation process of
pore structure in PDMS layer were shown in line 71-72 in the main text and
Supplementary Fig.4 in revised Supplementary Information with yellow highlight.
3.2 Why did longer TMC soaking result in “damages the integrity of membrane
structure”? Does this mean more pore structures formed or degradation to the PDMS
polymer?
Reply: We agree with the reviewer’s comments. Longer TMC-solution soaking will
intensify the swelling of the PDMS layer, which will further enlarge segment distance
and produce more micropores based on solvent-induced swelling mechanism (see the
response in Question 3.1). Excessive swelling will inevitably dissolve partial PDMS
segments, even cause microscopic cracks or complete rupture, resulting in a decrease
of CO /N separation ability (Fig.R1).
2 2
Fig. R1 The CO /N separation performance of mPSf membrane with soaking time. In the
2 2
fabrication of the crumpled membrane, the TMC-solution soaking time was controlled within 3 min.
4. The authors did not understand my question about nanoindentation. What is the film
thickness of the crumpled film at the valleys? If the film thickness at the valley is very
small, the measurements are significantly affected by the substrate, which is widely
acknowledged as the “substrate effect”. The other thing that the authors need to be
aware of is that the tip radius is typically 20–100 nm. That means at indentation depths
<10 nm, the measured response is dominated by the blunted tip apex rather than the
designed geometry. This affects the contact area calculation which often leads to errors
in hardness and modulus extraction. This is known as the “surface effect”.
Reply: We fully agree with and sincerely thank the reviewer for these critical insights
about “substrate effect” and the “surface effect” in nanoindentation measurements.
The thickness of the valleys (~65 nm) is the same as that at the peaks. To minimize the
influence of the substrate, the indentation depth should be less than 10~20% of the total
thickness to avoid the “substrate effect” from previous reports (Nanoscale Res. Lett. 2011, 6, 270; J Mater. Res. 1992, 7, 1564; Langmuir 1999, 15, 5630). In this work, the
maximum indentation depth was still below 6 nm, which is less than 10% of the total
thickness at valleys. Hence, this ensures that the measured modulus is dominated by
the properties of the valley.
We fully agree with the reviewer that the use of a nominal tip radius is insufficient,
especially at indentation depths (<10 nm) where the measured response is dominated
by the blunted tip apex. In fact, we have noticed this issue you mentioned. Hence, both
before and after testing, we have calibrated the tip radius and used the calibrated value
instead of nominal tip radius to measure the Young’s modulus of all the samples, which
can effectively eliminate the influence of tip blunting on the results. This calibrated tip
radius (35±3 nm), which accounts for tip blunting, was used for all subsequent contact
area calculations and modulus extractions from our samples. The details were shown in
line 473-478 in Methods with yellow highlight.

crumpled structure. In this work, squeeze peaks onto the support under a high force can
guarantee the test condition is consistent with that at valleys. Young’s modulus is a

Meanwhile, the change of Young’s modulus of PA-type materials with structures has
been confirmed by many researches (Int. J Solids Struct. 2022, 239, 111419; Compos.

The reviewer rightly points out that indentation measurements on thin films must be
conducted in the elastic regime where the substrate effect is negligible. To minimize
the influence of the substrate, the indentation depth should be less than 10~20% of the
total thickness to avoid the “substrate effect” from previous reports (Nanoscale Res.
Lett. 2011, 6, 270; J Mater. Res. 1992, 7, 1564; Langmuir 1999, 15, 5630). In this work,

membrane surface, which changes with the attached force. Above explanations were
shown in line 214-216 in revised main text, and Supplementary Fig.43a in revised
Supplementary Information with yellow highlight.

2

2

2 2

2

2

TEM images, image contrasts originate from the variations of the detecting thickness
(not membrane thickness) caused by the peak and valley structures. The larger the
detecting thickness of a local region, the darker it appears on the TEM image as less
electrons are transmitted due to scattering. Therefore, in Supplementary Fig.3d, bright
regions correspond to peak structures, while dark regions match valley structures

aspects.
